statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let q_1,q_3:X^3\to X be the projections, let p_{13}:X^3\to X\times X, and let p_1,p_2:X\times X\to X. Let C be a d-cycle on X^3 and m an integer. If for every integral component T of C one has \dim q_1 T+\dim q_3 T\le d+m, then for every integral component V of the pushforward cycle p_{13*}C one has \dim p_1 V+\dim p_2 V\le d+m.
proof: Write C = sum_{i=1}^r n_i [T_i], where the T_i are the distinct integral closed subschemes of X^3 of dimension d occurring in C and n_i are nonzero integers. If C=0, then p_{13*}C=0 and there are no integral components V, so the assertion is vacuous; assume C is nonzero. The morphism p_{13}: X^3 -> X x X, (x_1,x_2,x_3) -> (x_1,x_3), is proper: after the canonical isomorphism X^3 = (X x X) x X, it is the projection (X x X) x X -> X x X, which is projective because X/k is projective. For each i let W_i = p_{13}(T_i) with the reduced structure. Since p_{13} is proper, W_i is a closed subset of X x X; since T_i is integral, W_i is irreducible, hence with the reduced structure W_i is an integral closed subscheme. Also dim W_i <= dim T_i = d. By the definition of pushforward of cycles for a proper morphism, p_{13*}[T_i] = deg(k(T_i)/k(W_i)) [W_i] if dim W_i = d, and p_{13*}[T_i] = 0 if dim W_i < d. When dim W_i = d, the degree is a positive integer: the morphism T_i -> W_i is dominant, k(T_i) is algebraic over k(W_i) because the transcendence degrees over k are equal, and k(T_i) is finitely generated over k, so this algebraic extension is finite. Let I_d = {i : dim W_i = d}. Then p_{13*}C = sum_{i in I_d} n_i deg(k(T_i)/k(W_i)) [W_i]. Grouping equal W_i, we can write p_{13*}C = sum_V c_V [V], where the sum is over integral closed subschemes V of X x X of dimension d and c_V is the sum of the nonzero integers n_i deg(k(T_i)/k(W_i)) over i in I_d with W_i = V. An integral component V of the cycle p_{13*}C is precisely a V with c_V != 0. For such V choose i in I_d with W_i = V; then n_i deg(k(T_i)/k(W_i)) is nonzero. For this i, p_1(V) = p_1(W_i) = p_1(p_{13}(T_i)) = (p_1 p_{13})(T_i) = q_1(T_i) as subsets of X, and similarly p_2(V) = q_3(T_i), because p_1 p_{13} = q_1 and p_2 p_{13} = q_3. The maps p_1: X x X -> X and q_1: X^3 -> X are proper projections, so these images are closed subsets of X; since they coincide as sets, dim p_1 V = dim q_1 T_i. Similarly dim p_2 V = dim q_3 T_i. The hypothesis applied to the integral component T_i of C gives dim q_1 T_i + dim q_3 T_i <= d + m. Therefore dim p_1 V + dim p_2 V <= d + m. Since V was arbitrary, the claim follows.

statement: Let Y/k be a smooth projective variety, let M=Y x_k A^1_k, and let eta=Spec k(t) be the generic point of A^1_k. For a closed point s of A^1_k let i_s:Y x_k Spec kappa(s) -> M be the closed immersion. Then for every n>=0, every gamma in CH^n(M) with integral coefficients whose flat pullback to Y x_k eta is zero is a finite sum of classes i_{s*} delta_s with delta_s in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s)).
proof:
Let Y/k be a smooth projective variety, M = Y x_k A^1_k, eta = Spec k(t) the generic point of A^1_k, and n >= 0. Let gamma be in CH^n(M) with integral coefficients such that the flat pullback of gamma to Y x_k eta is zero. We must show that gamma is a finite sum of classes i_{s*}(delta_s) with delta_s in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s)).

Step 1 (Reduction to a principal open by lemma_61). By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_61, since the flat pullback of gamma to Y x_k eta is zero, there exists a nonzero polynomial f in k[t] such that the flat pullback of gamma to Y x_k D(f) is zero in CH^n(Y x_k D(f)), where D(f) is the principal open subset of A^1_k on which f does not vanish.

Step 2 (Setup of the closed and open subsets). Let Z' be the reduced closed subset of A^1_k defined by the vanishing of f. Since f is a nonzero element of k[t], the ideal (f) in k[t] is proper and the quotient k[t]/(f) is a finite-dimensional k-algebra; its nilradical is the product of the maximal ideals corresponding to the distinct irreducible factors of f. Hence Z' = Spec(k[t]/(f))_red is a finite disjoint union of spectra of finite field extensions of k, i.e., Z' = {s_1, ..., s_r} as a reduced closed subset, where s_1, ..., s_r are the distinct closed points of A^1_k at which f vanishes, and r >= 0 (with r = 0 precisely when f is a nonzero constant, in which case Z' is the empty scheme). Define W = Y x_k Z' and U = Y x_k D(f). Since D(f) = A^1_k \ Z' as topological spaces, we have U = M \ W. The closed immersion i: W -> M and the open immersion j: U -> M satisfy: i has codimension 1 (because dim W = dim Y = dim M - 1, since Z' has codimension 1 in A^1_k); j is flat (open immersions are flat). The flat pullback of gamma to Y x_k D(f) = U is exactly j^*(gamma) in CH^n(U), so by Step 1 we have j^*(gamma) = 0.

Step 3 (The localization sequence). We prove the following claim, which is the localization exact sequence for the pair (W, U) in M.

Claim. The sequence CH^{n-1}(W) --i_*--> CH^n(M) --j^*--> CH^n(U) -> 0 is exact, where i_*: CH^{n-1}(W) -> CH^n(M) is the pushforward of cycles along the codimension-1 closed immersion i: W -> M, and j^*: CH^n(M) -> CH^n(U) is the flat pullback (restriction of cycles) along the open immersion j: U -> M.

Proof of the claim. We verify surjectivity of j^* and exactness at CH^n(M).

(a) Surjectivity of j^*. Let [Z] be an arbitrary class in CH^n(U). It is represented by a formal sum of integral closed subschemes of U of codimension n; by linearity it suffices to treat the case where Z is a single integral closed subscheme of U of codimension n. Let Zbar be the scheme-theoretic closure of Z in M. Since U is open and dense in M (D(f) is open and dense in A^1_k, and Y is the same in both), and Z has pure codimension n in U, the closure Zbar has pure codimension n in M: indeed, for any irreducible component T of Zbar, T is the closure of T ∩ U (an irreducible component of Z), and codim_M(T) = codim_U(T ∩ U) = n because U is open in M and T ∩ U is dense in T. Moreover, Zbar ∩ U = Z as schemes: Z is closed in U, and Zbar is the smallest closed subscheme of M containing Z, so Zbar ∩ U is the smallest closed subscheme of U containing Z, which is Z itself. The restriction of the cycle Zbar to U is Zbar ∩ U = Z (as a cycle, since Zbar is integral and not contained in W = M \ U). Hence j^*([Zbar]) = [Zbar ∩ U] = [Z]. This proves j^* is surjective.

(b) Exactness at CH^n(M). Let gamma' be a class in CH^n(M) with j^*(gamma') = 0. We show gamma' lies in the image of i_*.

Choose a cycle representative Z' = sum_{j} n_j Z_j of gamma', where the Z_j range over the distinct integral closed subschemes of M of codimension n that appear, with nonzero integer coefficients n_j. Partition the summands into two groups: those Z_j not contained in W (call the resulting sub-cycle Z'_U) and those Z_j contained in W (call the resulting sub-cycle Z'_W). Thus Z' = Z'_U + Z'_W, where Z'_U is an n-codimensional cycle in U and Z'_W is an n-codimensional cycle supported in W.

The restriction j^*(Z') equals Z'_U (the part of Z' lying in U). Since j^*(gamma') = 0, the class [Z'_U] is zero in CH^n(U), i.e., Z'_U is rationally equivalent to zero in U.

Subcase n = 0. Then Z'_U is a zero-codimensional cycle in U, i.e., a formal sum of irreducible components of U. Since M is irreducible (Y is a variety, hence irreducible, and A^1_k is irreducible, so M = Y x_k A^1_k is irreducible), and U is a nonempty open subset of M, U is irreducible. Hence Z'_U = m · U for a unique integer m. The group CH^0(U) is the free abelian group on the irreducible components of U modulo rational equivalence; since U is irreducible, CH^0(U) = Z · [U]. The class [Z'_U] = m · [U] is zero if and only if m = 0. Hence Z'_U = 0, so Z' = Z'_W. But Z' is a zero-codimensional cycle in M, so Z' = m' · M for some integer m' (the only zero-codimensional subvariety of the irreducible scheme M is M itself). Since M is not contained in W (W is a proper closed subset of M, as Z' is a proper closed subset of A^1_k because f is nonzero), we have Z'_W = 0. Thus m' = 0 and Z' = 0, so gamma' = 0. On the other hand, CH^{-1}(W) = 0 (there are no subvarieties of codimension -1 in any scheme), so im(i_*) = 0. Hence gamma' = 0 lies in im(i_*), and exactness holds in this subcase.

Subcase n >= 1. Since Z'_U is rationally equivalent to zero in U and n >= 1, by the definition of rational equivalence for n-codimensional cycles there exist integral closed subschemes V_1, ..., V_m of U of codimension n-1 and rational functions f_l in the function field of V_l (l = 1, ..., m) such that Z'_U = sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_l}(f_l), where div_{V_l}(f_l) denotes the Weil divisor of f_l on V_l, viewed as an n-codimensional cycle in U. (If m = 0, the sum is the zero cycle.)

For each l = 1, ..., m, let V_lbar be the scheme-theoretic closure of V_l in M. As in part (a), V_lbar is an integral closed subscheme of M of codimension n-1, and V_lbar ∩ U = V_l. The rational function f_l on V_l identifies with a rational function on V_lbar (since V_l is dense in V_lbar, the function fields k(V_l) and k(V_lbar) are equal). The Weil divisor div_{V_lbar}(f_l) is an n-codimensional cycle on M (a formal sum of integral closed subschemes of V_lbar of codimension 1, hence of M of codimension n).

We claim that j^*(div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = div_{V_l}(f_l). To verify this, note that the integral components of div_{V_lbar}(f_l) are prime divisors of V_lbar, i.e., integral closed subschemes D of V_lbar of codimension 1 (equivalently, integral closed subschemes of M of codimension n contained in V_lbar). The component D is contained in W if and only if D is not contained in U, i.e., if and only if D is not a prime divisor of V_l = V_lbar ∩ U. For those D not contained in W, D is a prime divisor of V_l, and the coefficient of D in div_{V_lbar}(f_l) is the valuation v_D(f_l) computed in the discrete valuation ring O_{V_lbar, D}^{(1)} (the local ring of V_lbar at D, which is a DVR since D is a prime divisor of the integral scheme V_lbar). Since D is also a prime divisor of V_l and O_{V_l, D} = O_{V_lbar, D} (the local ring at D is the same whether we view D as a point of V_l or of V_lbar, because V_l is open in V_lbar), the valuation v_D(f_l) is the same. Hence the restriction of div_{V_lbar}(f_l) to U (i.e., the sum of those components not contained in W, with their coefficients) is exactly div_{V_l}(f_l). This proves j^*(div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = div_{V_l}(f_l).

By linearity of j^*, we obtain:
j^*(sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = sum_{l=1}^{m} j^*(div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_l}(f_l) = Z'_U.

Therefore:
j^*(Z' - sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = j^*(Z') - j^*(sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)) = Z'_U - Z'_U = 0.

Since j^* of the cycle Z' - sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l) is zero, every integral component of this cycle is contained in W (by the definition of j^* as restriction to U). Hence Z' - sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l) is an n-codimensional cycle on M whose support is contained in W. An n-codimensional cycle supported in W is equivalently an (n-1)-codimensional cycle on W (because W has codimension 1 in M: an integral closed subscheme of W of codimension n-1 in W is an integral closed subscheme of M of codimension n in M, and vice versa). Let delta be the class of this (n-1)-codimensional cycle in CH^{n-1}(W). Then i_*(delta) is the class in CH^n(M) of the same cycle, viewed as an n-codimensional cycle on M.

On the other hand, sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l) is rationally equivalent to zero in M: it is a sum of Weil divisors of rational functions on (n-1)-codimensional integral closed subschemes of M, which is precisely the definition of a rationally trivial n-codimensional cycle in M. Hence [sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)] = 0 in CH^n(M).

Combining these facts:
gamma' = [Z'] = [Z' - sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)] + [sum_{l=1}^{m} div_{V_lbar}(f_l)] = i_*(delta) + 0 = i_*(delta).

This proves gamma' lies in im(i_*), establishing exactness at CH^n(M) for n >= 1.

The claim is proved.

Step 4 (Application of the localization sequence). Since j^*(gamma) = 0 (by Step 1) and the sequence CH^{n-1}(W) --i_*--> CH^n(M) --j^*--> CH^n(U) -> 0 is exact (Step 3), there exists a class delta in CH^{n-1}(W) such that gamma = i_*(delta).

Step 5 (Decomposition of W into closed fibers). If r = 0 (i.e., f is a nonzero constant), then W is the empty scheme, CH^{n-1}(W) = 0, and delta = 0. Hence gamma = i_*(0) = 0, which is the empty sum of classes i_{s*}(delta_s). The desired conclusion holds trivially.

Assume r >= 1. The scheme W = Y x_k Z' is the finite disjoint union of the closed subschemes W_i = Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i) for i = 1, ..., r. We use the following standard fact: if X = X_1 disjoint union ... disjoint union X_r is a finite disjoint union of schemes, then CH^n(X) = CH^n(X_1) x ... x CH^n(X_r) (direct sum). Justification: an integral closed subscheme of X is contained in a unique X_i (since the X_i are disjoint and closed in X), so every cycle on X decomposes uniquely as a sum of cycles on the X_i; and a rational function on an integral closed subscheme V of X is a rational function on the unique X_i containing V, so the group of rational equivalences on X is the direct sum of the groups on the X_i. Hence CH^{n-1}(W) = direct sum_{i=1}^{r} CH^{n-1}(W_i) = direct sum_{i=1}^{r} CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i)).

Write delta = (delta_1, ..., delta_r) with delta_i in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i)) for each i. The pushforward i_*: CH^{n-1}(W) -> CH^n(M) is the sum of the pushforwards along the inclusions W_i -> W -> M, because the pushforward of a cycle on a disjoint union is the sum of the pushforwards of the cycles on the components. Concretely, if i_{s_i}: W_i = Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i) -> M denotes the closed immersion (which factors as W_i -> W --i--> M), then i_* = sum_{i=1}^{r} i_{s_i*}, where i_{s_i*}: CH^{n-1}(W_i) -> CH^n(M) is the pushforward along the codimension-1 closed immersion i_{s_i} (codimension 1 because dim W_i = dim Y = dim M - 1).

Therefore:
gamma = i_*(delta) = (sum_{i=1}^{r} i_{s_i*})(delta_1, ..., delta_r) = sum_{i=1}^{r} i_{s_i*}(delta_i),
where delta_i in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i)) for each i = 1, ..., r.

Step 6 (Conclusion). We have expressed gamma as the finite sum sum_{i=1}^{r} i_{s_i*}(delta_i) with delta_i in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s_i)). Renaming s_i as s and delta_i as delta_s, this is a finite sum of classes i_{s*}(delta_s) with delta_s in CH^{n-1}(Y x_k Spec kappa(s)), as required. This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let E/k be a finite extension of degree n, and let f: X_E x_E X_E -> X x X be the finite flat base-change morphism. For gamma in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients, suppose f^* gamma has a d-cycle representative Z_E on X_E x_E X_E such that for every integral component C of Z_E at least one of the two projections of C to X_E has dimension < d. Then n gamma has a d-cycle representative Z on X x X such that for every integral component C of Z at least one of the two projections of C to X has dimension < d.
proof:
Proof. Put Y = X x X, Y_E = X_E x_E X_E, and let f: Y_E -> Y be the projection. Since Spec E -> Spec k is finite flat of rank n, base change by Y shows that f is finite flat of rank n. Let p_1, p_2: Y -> X and p_{1,E}, p_{2,E}: Y_E -> X_E be the two projections, and let g: X_E -> X be the base-change map. Then p_i f = g p_{i,E} for i = 1,2. We use the standard fact that a finite morphism preserves the dimension of integral closed subsets: if h: U -> V is finite and U is an integral closed subset, then h(U) is an integral closed subset and dim h(U) = dim U, because the induced extension of function fields k(h(U)) in k(U) is finite.

We first prove a push-pull subclaim: for every d-cycle A on Y, f_* f^* A = n A as cycles. By linearity it is enough to prove this for A = [W], where W is an integral d-dimensional closed subscheme of Y. Set W' = f^{-1}(W) = W x_Y Y_E. Because f is finite flat of rank n, W' is finite flat of rank n over W, hence equidimensional of dimension d. Let V_1,...,V_r be the integral components of W', and let m_j be the multiplicity of V_j in the cycle associated to W', namely m_j = length of the local ring O_{W',V_j}. Since W' is finite flat over the integral scheme W, it is unmixed of dimension d, so the definition of flat pullback gives f^*[W] = sum_j m_j [V_j]. For each j, the image f(V_j) is an integral closed subset of W of dimension d by the finite-dimension fact, hence f(V_j) = W. Therefore f_*[V_j] = [k(V_j):k(W)] [W]. It follows that f_* f^*[W] = (sum_j m_j [k(V_j):k(W)]) [W].

We now compute the coefficient. Let K = k(W). The generic fiber A = O_{W'} tensor_{O_W} K is a finite-dimensional K-algebra of dimension n, because W' is finite flat of rank n over W. The local ring O_{W',V_j} is already a K-algebra, because the contraction of V_j to W is the generic point, so every nonzero element of O_W is invertible in O_{W',V_j}. It is an Artin local K-algebra with residue field k(V_j). For an Artin local K-algebra B with residue field k, a composition series of length length(B) has quotients isomorphic to k, so dim_K B = length(B) [k:K]. Hence dim_K O_{W',V_j} = m_j [k(V_j):K]. The Artin algebra A decomposes as the product of its localizations at its maximal ideals. The maximal ideals of A correspond to the primes of O_{W'} contracting to 0; since O_{W'} is finite over the domain O_W, these primes are exactly the minimal primes V_j. Localization commutes with tensor product, so the corresponding local factors of A are exactly O_{W',V_j}; thus dim_K A = sum_j m_j [k(V_j):K]. Since dim_K A = n, we get sum_j m_j [k(V_j):K] = n. Substituting K = k(W) proves f_* f^*[W] = n[W]. By linearity, f_* f^* A = n A for every d-cycle A, and passing to Chow groups gives f_* f^* alpha = n alpha for every alpha in CH^d(Y).

Now let Z_E be the given d-cycle on Y_E representing f^* gamma, and set Z = f_* Z_E. Write Z_E = sum_C m_C [C], where the C run over the integral components of Z_E. Because f is finite, Z is a d-cycle on Y: each f(C) is integral of dimension d, and f_*[C] = [k(C):k(f(C))] [f(C)], so Z = sum_C m_C [k(C):k(f(C))] [f(C)] with like terms combined.

We claim that every integral component D of Z has at least one projection of dimension < d. Let D be an integral component of Z. Then D = f(C) for some integral component C of Z_E. By hypothesis, either dim p_{1,E}(C) < d or dim p_{2,E}(C) < d. Suppose dim p_{1,E}(C) < d; the other case is identical. The projection p_{1,E} is proper, so p_{1,E}(C) is a closed integral subset of X_E. Using p_1 f = g p_{1,E}, we have p_1(D) = p_1(f(C)) = g(p_{1,E}(C)). The morphism g: X_E -> X is finite, so by the finite-dimension fact dim g(p_{1,E}(C)) = dim p_{1,E}(C). Therefore dim p_1(D) < d. Thus D satisfies the required condition.

Finally, because f is proper, it induces a pushforward homomorphism on Chow groups, so the class of Z depends only on the rational equivalence class of Z_E. Hence [Z] = f_*[Z_E] = f_* f^* gamma = n gamma in CH^d(Y). Thus Z is a d-cycle representative of n gamma such that for every integral component D of Z at least one of the two projections of D to X has dimension < d. This completes the proof.

statement: Let Y be a smooth projective variety of dimension d over a field, and let p_1,p_2:Y x Y -> Y be the projections. For a d-cycle Z=sum_i n_i Z_i on Y x Y set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d), lev(0)=-1, and for gamma in CH^d(Y x Y) let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Then the set of gamma with ell(gamma) <= d-1 is an additive subgroup of CH^d(Y x Y).
proof:
Proof. Let X = Y x_k Y and let p_1,p_2 be the projections. We first prove the dimension inequality that was missing in the earlier attempt, using function fields; this replaces the faulty finite-module argument.

Step 1. Let W be an integral closed subscheme of X. Put A = p_1(W) with its reduced structure and B = p_2(W) with its reduced structure. Because Y is projective, p_1 and p_2 are proper, so A and B are closed integral subschemes of Y of finite type over k. Let K = k(W), K_A = k(A), K_B = k(B) be the function fields. Let eta, eta_A, eta_B be the generic points. Since W is irreducible, p_1(W) is irreducible; the closure of p_1(eta) is p_1(W), so p_1(eta) = eta_A. Similarly p_2(eta) = eta_B. Hence p_1|_W : W -> A and p_2|_W : W -> B are dominant. For a dominant morphism of integral schemes the induced map on function fields is injective: affine locally at the generic points the source local ring is a field, and the kernel of the map from the target function field is an ideal of a field, not the whole field because 1 maps to 1. Thus K_A and K_B embed in K.

We claim K is the compositum k(K_A,K_B) inside K. Choose affine open neighborhoods U = Spec R of eta_A in Y and V = Spec S of eta_B in Y. Then U x_k V = Spec(R tensor_k S) is an affine open neighborhood of eta in X. The point eta corresponds to a prime ideal q of R tensor_k S, and K = Frac((R tensor_k S)/q). Let a = ker(R -> (R tensor_k S)/q) and b = ker(S -> (R tensor_k S)/q). The images of R/a and S/b in (R tensor_k S)/q generate it as a k-algebra, because R tensor_k S is generated as a k-algebra by the two factor images r -> r tensor 1 and s -> 1 tensor s. Moreover a defines the closed subscheme of U whose underlying set is the closure of p_1(W cap (U x_k V)); since this closure contains eta_A and A cap U is closed in U, it is exactly A cap U. Thus Frac(R/a) = K_A. Similarly Frac(S/b) = K_B. Passing to fraction fields gives K = k(K_A,K_B).

Now use the standard fact that for an integral scheme of finite type over k, dimension equals the transcendence degree of its function field over k. Thus dim W = trdeg_k K, dim A = trdeg_k K_A, dim B = trdeg_k K_B. If T_A and T_B are transcendence bases of K_A and K_B over k, then K is algebraic over k(T_A union T_B); hence trdeg_k K <= |T_A| + |T_B|. Therefore dim W <= dim A + dim B = dim p_1(W) + dim p_2(W). This is the required inequality, proved without asserting dim B = dim A for a finite module.

Step 2. Let Z be a d-cycle on X. If Z = 0, lev(Z) = -1 by definition. If Z != 0, every integral component W of Z has dimension d. By Step 1, dim p_1(W) + dim p_2(W) >= d, so each summand dim p_1(W)+dim p_2(W)-d in lev(Z) is >=0. Hence lev(Z) >=0. In particular lev takes values in {-1,0,1,...}. For the zero class 0 in CH^d(X), the zero cycle is a representative with lev = -1, and every nonzero representative has lev >=0; therefore ell(0) = -1. Also, for every class gamma, the set of values lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma is a nonempty subset of the integers bounded below, so the minimum defining ell(gamma) is attained.

Step 3. Let S = { gamma in CH^d(X) : ell(gamma) <= d-1 }. We prove S is an additive subgroup.

Identity: ell(0) = -1 <= d-1, so 0 in S. (Here d >= 0; if d=0 this reads -1 <= -1.)

Negation: Let gamma in S. Since ell(gamma) <= d-1, there is a d-cycle representative Z of gamma with lev(Z) = ell(gamma) <= d-1. The cycle -Z represents -gamma and has the same integral components as Z, so lev(-Z) = lev(Z) <= d-1. Hence ell(-gamma) <= d-1.

Addition: Let gamma, delta in S. Choose representatives Z, Z' with lev(Z) <= d-1 and lev(Z') <= d-1. The formal sum Z + Z' is a d-cycle representative of gamma + delta. We show lev(Z+Z') <= max(lev(Z),lev(Z')). If Z+Z' = 0, then lev(Z+Z') = -1 and there is nothing to check. Otherwise let W be an integral component of Z+Z' with nonzero coefficient. Then W occurs with nonzero coefficient in Z or in Z' (or both). If it occurs in Z, then dim p_1(W)+dim p_2(W)-d <= lev(Z); if it occurs in Z', the same quantity is <= lev(Z'). Thus for every component W of Z+Z', dim p_1(W)+dim p_2(W)-d <= max(lev(Z),lev(Z')). Taking the maximum over W gives lev(Z+Z') <= max(lev(Z),lev(Z')) <= d-1. Therefore ell(gamma+delta) <= d-1.

Thus S contains 0 and is closed under negation and addition, so it is an additive subgroup of CH^d(X). This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let γ∈CH^d(X×_k X) be torsion, let m≥1 be an integer with mγ=0, and let L/k be a finite extension of degree n with gcd(n,m)=1. Denote by γ_L the flat pullback of γ in CH^d(X_L×_L X_L). If every d-cycle representative of γ has an integral component whose two projections to X have dimension d, then every d-cycle representative of γ_L has an integral component whose two projections to X_L have dimension d.
proof:
Let Y = X \times_k X and Y_L = X_L \times_L X_L, and let f: Y_L \to Y be the finite flat base-change morphism f = id_X \times_k id_{Spec L}; it has degree n = [L:k]. Write p_1, p_2: Y \to X for the two projections and p_1^L, p_2^L: Y_L \to X_L for the two projections of Y_L. By definition \gamma_L = f^*\gamma \in CH^d(Y_L).

We prove the implication by contradiction. Suppose the hypothesis holds:
(H) every d-cycle representative of \gamma on Y has an integral component V with dim p_1(V) = dim p_2(V) = d.
Suppose, toward a contradiction, that the conclusion fails: there exists a d-cycle representative Z_E of \gamma_L on Y_L such that for every integral component C of Z_E one has dim p_1^L(C) < d or dim p_2^L(C) < d. (The case Z_E = 0 is included: the zero cycle has no integral components, so the condition holds vacuously.)

Step 1 (descent). Apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/1361a0 with E = L (hence degree n = [L:k]) and the same \gamma \in CH^d(X \times_k X). Its hypothesis is exactly the existence of the cycle Z_E just described, and its conclusion yields a d-cycle representative Z of n\gamma on Y = X \times_k X such that for every integral component C of Z one has dim p_1(C) < d or dim p_2(C) < d. In other words, Z has no integral component whose two projections to X both have dimension d. (When d = 0 this forces Z = 0, since no nonempty variety has dimension < 0, i.e. n\gamma = 0; the argument below is uniform in d.)

Step 2 (Bezout). Since gcd(n, m) = 1, Bezout's identity gives integers a, b with an + bm = 1. Multiplying by \gamma and using m\gamma = 0:
\gamma = (an + bm)\gamma = a(n\gamma) + b(m\gamma) = a(n\gamma).

Step 3 (a \neq 0). We claim a \neq 0. If a = 0, then bm = 1; as b, m \in Z this forces m = 1 (and b = 1). But m\gamma = 0 with m = 1 gives \gamma = 0, so the zero cycle 0 on Y is a d-cycle representative of \gamma = 0. It has no integral components at all, hence no integral component whose two projections to X both have dimension d, contradicting (H). Therefore a \neq 0.

Step 4 (scale Z). Write Z = \sum_i n_i V_i with the V_i distinct integral d-dimensional closed subvarieties of Y and n_i \in Z \setminus {0}. The cycle aZ = \sum_i (a n_i) V_i is a d-cycle on Y. Because a \neq 0, a n_i \neq 0 for every i, so the integral components of aZ are exactly the V_i, the same integral subvarieties as those of Z; in particular for each i the projections p_1(V_i), p_2(V_i) are unchanged. The cycle-class map Z_d(Y) \twoheadrightarrow CH^d(Y) (the quotient of the free abelian group on integral d-subvarieties by the subgroup of rationally trivial cycles) is a surjective group homomorphism, so [aZ] = a[Z] = a(n\gamma) = \gamma in CH^d(Y); thus aZ is a d-cycle representative of \gamma. By Step 1, for every integral component V_i of aZ one has dim p_1(V_i) < d or dim p_2(V_i) < d. Hence aZ is a d-cycle representative of \gamma with no integral component whose two projections to X both have dimension d, contradicting (H).

The contradiction shows that the assumption that the conclusion fails is impossible. Therefore every d-cycle representative of \gamma_L on Y_L has an integral component whose two projections to X_L both have dimension d, which is the desired conclusion.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, let K be the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X×X)→CH^d(X_L×X_L), and let p_1,p_2:X×X→X be the projections. For a d-cycle W=∑ n_i W_i on X×X set lev(W)=max_i(dim p_1 W_i+dim p_2 W_i-d), lev(0)=-1, and for γ∈CH^d(X×X) let ℓ(γ) be the minimum of lev(W) over d-cycle representatives W of γ. For each integer p with 0≤p≤d+1, the set F^p={α∈K | ℓ(α)≤d-p} is an additive subgroup of K.
proof: Let φ: CH^d(X×X) → CH^d(X_L×X_L) be the flat pullback and K=ker(φ). For α,β∈K we have φ(α+β)=φ(α)+φ(β)=0 and φ(−α)=−φ(α)=0, so K is an additive subgroup of CH^d(X×X). Fix p with 0≤p≤d+1. We show F^p={α∈K | ℓ(α)≤d−p} is an additive subgroup of K. First, 0∈F^p. The zero cycle 0 is a representative of 0 and lev(0)=−1 by definition. If W=Σ n_i W_i is any nonzero d-cycle on X×X, each integral component W_i has dimension d. Since W_i⊂p_1(W_i)×p_2(W_i), we have d=dim W_i≤dim p_1(W_i)+dim p_2(W_i); hence dim p_1(W_i)+dim p_2(W_i)−d≥0 for every i, so lev(W)≥0. Therefore the minimum defining ℓ(0) is −1. Because p≤d+1, d−p≥−1, so ℓ(0)≤d−p. Next, let α∈F^p. The operation W↦−W is a bijection between d-cycle representatives of α and d-cycle representatives of −α, and lev(−W)=lev(W): for W=0 this is the convention lev(0)=−1, and for W=Σ n_i W_i the cycle −W=Σ(−n_i)W_i has exactly the same integral components W_i, so the projection dimensions are unchanged. Taking minima gives ℓ(−α)=ℓ(α)≤d−p. Since K is a subgroup, −α∈K, hence −α∈F^p. Finally, let α,β∈F^p. Then α+β∈K. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_44, ℓ(α+β)≤max(ℓ(α),ℓ(β)). Since α,β∈F^p, ℓ(α)≤d−p and ℓ(β)≤d−p, so max(ℓ(α),ℓ(β))≤d−p. Thus ℓ(α+β)≤d−p, and α+β∈F^p. We have shown that F^p contains 0 and is closed under addition and inverses; therefore F^p is an additive subgroup of K.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, and let p_1,p_2:X×X→X be the projections. For a d-cycle Z on X×X, let Z_top be the sum, with multiplicities, of the integral components C of Z with dim p_1(C)=dim p_2(C)=d, and let τ(Z)=(p_1*Z_top,p_2*Z_top)∈Z^2, identifying p_1*Z_top and p_2*Z_top with integers via CH_d(X)≅Z. If Z and Z' are d-cycles on X×X such that Z-Z' is a d-cycle all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1(C)+dim p_2(C)≤2d-1, then τ(Z)=τ(Z').
proof:
Proof. We argue purely at the level of cycles (formal sums of integral closed subvarieties); the only input beyond the definitions is the identification CH_d(X) = Z that appears in the definition of tau. No Chow-theoretic fact about rational equivalence is used.

Step 1 (notation). Write Z = sum_i n_i C_i and Z' = sum_j m_j D_j as formal sums over their distinct integral components, where the C_i (resp. D_j) are the integral d-dimensional subvarieties of X x X appearing in Z (resp. Z') and n_i, m_j in Z are nonzero. For an integral d-dimensional subvariety C contained in X x X, let nu(C) in Z be its multiplicity in Z (nu(C)=0 if C is not a component of Z) and mu(C) in Z its multiplicity in Z' (mu(C)=0 if C is not a component of Z'). Then, in the free abelian group Z_d(X x X) of d-cycles on X x X, Z - Z' = sum_C (nu(C) - mu(C)) C, where the sum ranges over all integral d-dimensional subvarieties C contained in X x X with nu(C)!=0 or mu(C)!=0. The integral components of Z - Z' are exactly those C for which nu(C) - mu(C) != 0.

Step 2 (dimension bound). For any integral component C of a d-cycle on X x X we have dim p_1(C) <= d and dim p_2(C) <= d. Indeed, p_1(C) is the image of the irreducible set C under the morphism p_1, hence an irreducible subset of X; its closure in X is an irreducible closed subset of X of dimension at most dim X = d, and dim p_1(C) equals the dimension of that closure, hence is <= d. The same argument gives dim p_2(C) <= d. Consequently dim p_1(C) + dim p_2(C) <= 2d, with equality if and only if dim p_1(C) = dim p_2(C) = d, i.e. if and only if C is a top component in the sense of the statement.

Step 3 (top components of Z and Z' agree with multiplicities). Let C contained in X x X be an integral d-dimensional subvariety with dim p_1(C) = dim p_2(C) = d. We claim nu(C) = mu(C). Suppose to the contrary that nu(C) - mu(C) != 0. Then, by Step 1, C is an integral component of Z - Z'. By the hypothesis on Z - Z' we get dim p_1(C) + dim p_2(C) <= 2d - 1. But by the choice of C and Step 2, dim p_1(C) + dim p_2(C) = d + d = 2d. Since 2d > 2d - 1, this is a contradiction. Hence nu(C) = mu(C).

Step 4 (Z_top = Z'_top). By definition Z_top = sum_{C top} nu(C) C and Z'_top = sum_{C top} mu(C) C, where 'C top' ranges over the integral d-dimensional subvarieties C contained in X x X with dim p_1(C) = dim p_2(C) = d (a C that is not a component contributes coefficient 0). By Step 3, nu(C) = mu(C) for every top C. The two formal sums are therefore identical: Z_top = Z'_top in Z_d(X x X).

Step 5 (pushforwards agree). The pushforward p_1*: Z_d(X x X) -> Z_d(X) on cycles is a group homomorphism: on a generator [C] with C an integral d-dimensional subvariety of X x X it is p_1*[C] = deg(k(C)/k(p_1(C))) [p_1(C)] when dim p_1(C) = d, and p_1*[C] = 0 when dim p_1(C) < d, and it extends linearly. Since Z_top = Z'_top as elements of Z_d(X x X), applying the homomorphism p_1* gives p_1*Z_top = p_1*Z'_top in Z_d(X). The identical argument with p_2 gives p_2*Z_top = p_2*Z'_top in Z_d(X).

Step 6 (conclusion). By definition tau(Z) = (deg(p_1*Z_top), deg(p_2*Z_top)) and tau(Z') = (deg(p_1*Z'_top), deg(p_2*Z'_top)), where deg: CH_d(X) -> Z is the isomorphism used to identify d-cycles on X with integers (the degree). From Step 5, p_1*Z_top and p_1*Z'_top are equal as cycles, hence represent the same class in CH_d(X); applying the well-defined function deg to equal classes gives equal integers, so the first coordinates of tau(Z) and tau(Z') agree. The same argument with p_2 shows the second coordinates agree. Therefore tau(Z) = tau(Z') in Z^2.

Edge cases. If d = 0, then X is 0-dimensional and every integral component C of a 0-cycle on X x X satisfies dim p_1(C) = dim p_2(C) = 0 = d, so every component is top. The hypothesis then reads: every integral component of Z - Z' satisfies 0 + 0 <= -1, which is impossible unless Z - Z' has no integral components, i.e. unless Z = Z'. Step 3 still applies verbatim: for any top C with nu(C) != mu(C), C would be a component of Z - Z' and the hypothesis would force 0 <= -1, a contradiction; hence nu(C) = mu(C) for all C and Z_top = Z'_top. If Z - Z' = 0, the hypothesis is vacuous and Step 3 gives nu(C) = mu(C) for every top C directly (if they differed, C would be a nonzero component of Z - Z', contradicting Z - Z' = 0). The argument is thus uniform in d and covers all edge conditions.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let k be a field, let A be a nonzero finitely generated k-algebra, and put r = dim A. Then there exist a finite field extension E/k and elements y_1, ..., y_r in A_E = A ⊗_k E such that A_E is finite as a module over E[y_1, ..., y_r].
proof: We prove the assertion by induction on n, where A is presented as k[x_1,...,x_n]/I with I proper. First we record an auxiliary claim. Claim. Let D be a nonzero commutative ring, and let D -> C be an injective homomorphism of commutative rings such that C is a finite D-module. Then dim C = dim D. Proof of claim. We first note that C is integral over D. Choose D-generators c_1,...,c_m of C. For c in C let T:C->C be multiplication by c. Write T(c_j)=sum_i a_{ij} c_i and let A=(a_{ij}). Let p(T)=det(T I_m - A)=T^m + t_1 T^{m-1}+...+t_m with t_i in D. The adjugate identity (T I_m - A) adj(T I_m - A)=p(T) I_m, viewed as a polynomial identity in T, implies A^m + t_1 A^{m-1}+...+t_m I_m=0. Hence (T^m + t_1 T^{m-1}+...+t_m I_C)(c_j)=0 for all j, so c^m + t_1 c^{m-1}+...+t_m c=0. Thus c is integral over D. Now we prove lying over, going up, and incomparability for this integral extension. Lying over: let p be a prime of D and let S be the complement of p in D. The localization S^{-1}C is a nonzero finite S^{-1}D-algebra. It is nonzero because if it were zero, then 1/1=0, so some s in S would annihilate 1_C; injectivity of D->C would force s=0 in D, but 0 is in p and hence not in S. Let M be a maximal ideal of S^{-1}C and let N be M intersect S^{-1}D. The ring S^{-1}C/M is a field integral over S^{-1}D/N, and S^{-1}D/N is a domain; a domain R over which a field K is integral is a field, because for a nonzero r in R, the element r^{-1} in K is integral over R, so r^{-n}+a_{n-1}r^{-(n-1)}+...+a_0=0, and multiplying by r^n gives r^{-1} in R. Thus N is maximal in S^{-1}D. Since S^{-1}D is local with maximal ideal pS^{-1}D, N=pS^{-1}D. Then M intersect D=p, giving a prime of C over p. Going up: if p is contained in p' in D and q is a prime of C over p, take S to be the complement of p' in D. The ideal qS^{-1}C is proper because q intersect D=p is contained in p'. Extend it to a maximal ideal M of S^{-1}C. As above, the contraction of M to S^{-1}D is maximal, hence p'S^{-1}D. Then q'=M intersect C is a prime over p' and contains q. Incomparability: suppose q is strictly contained in q' in C and q intersect D=q' intersect D=p. Localize at S, the complement of p in D. The ideals qS^{-1}C and q'S^{-1}C are prime ideals over the maximal ideal pS^{-1}D of S^{-1}D; each quotient by such a prime is a domain integral over the field S^{-1}D/(pS^{-1}D), hence a field, so both ideals are maximal, and therefore equal. If a is in q', then a/1 is in qS^{-1}C, so s a=b for some s in S and b in q. Since s is not in p=q intersect D, s is not in q; q is prime and b is in q, so a is in q. Thus q'=q, contradiction. Finally, any chain of primes in D lifts to a chain of primes in C by lying over and successive going up, so dim D <= dim C. Any chain of primes in C contracts to a chain of primes in D by incomparability, so dim C <= dim D. This proves the claim. End of claim. Now the induction. Base n=0: then A=k, r=0, and E=k works with no y_i. For n>=1, if I=0 then A=k[x_1,...,x_n] has dimension n, and E=k with y_i=x_i for i=1,...,n works. Assume I is nonzero. Choose f in I with f not 0 and let D=deg f. Permute the variables so that the top homogeneous part of f involves x_n; then f has positive degree in x_n. Write f=sum_{j=0}^N a_j x_n^j with N>=1, a_j in k[x_1,...,x_{n-1}], and a_N not 0. For each j, let F_{D-j}(a_j) denote the homogeneous part of a_j of degree D-j, with the convention that it is 0 if D-j<0 or if a_j has no part of that degree. Define H(t_1,...,t_{n-1})=sum_{j=0}^N F_{D-j}(a_j)(t_1,...,t_{n-1}) in k[t_1,...,t_{n-1}] (which is k when n=1). The polynomial H is not zero: the top homogeneous part of f is sum_{j=0}^N F_{D-j}(a_j) x_n^j, which is not zero, so at least one summand in H is nonzero; the summands have distinct degrees D-j, so they cannot cancel. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_63 applied to the domain k[t_1,...,t_{n-1}] and the nonzero element H, there is a finite field extension E_0/k and elements c_1,...,c_{n-1} in E_0 such that h=H(c_1,...,c_{n-1}) is not 0 in E_0. Let A_{E_0}=A tensor_k E_0. In A_{E_0} define y_n to be the image of x_n and y_i to be the image of x_i - c_i x_n for i<n. Equivalently, under the invertible linear change x_i=y_i+c_i y_n (i<n) and x_n=y_n, the ring A_{E_0} is isomorphic to E_0[y_1,...,y_n]/J for a proper ideal J. Let B be the image of E_0[y_1,...,y_{n-1}] in A_{E_0}. Substitute x_i=y_i+c_i y_n into f. The coefficient of y_n^D in the substituted polynomial is h. Indeed, for each j, the part of a_j(y_1+c_1 y_n,...,y_{n-1}+c_{n-1} y_n) having y_n-degree D-j is F_{D-j}(a_j)(c_1,...,c_{n-1}), and multiplying by y_n^j gives a y_n^D term; summing over j gives h. No term can have y_n-degree greater than D because f has total degree D. Thus f' = h y_n^D + sum_{e=0}^{D-1} b_e y_n^e with b_e in E_0[y_1,...,y_{n-1}]. Since f is in I, f' is 0 in A_{E_0}. The images of the b_e lie in B, and h is a unit of E_0, so y_n satisfies the monic equation y_n^D + b'_{D-1} y_n^{D-1}+...+b'_0=0 over B. Hence y_n is integral over B. Because A_{E_0} is generated over B by y_n and y_n satisfies a monic relation of degree D, A_{E_0} is a finite B-module, generated by 1,y_n,...,y_n^{D-1}. We now compare dimensions. The map A -> A_{E_0}, a -> a tensor 1, is injective. To see this, choose a k-basis e_1=1,...,e_m of E_0 and write a as a finite k-linear combination a=sum_j lambda_j a_j of elements a_j from a k-basis of A; the tensors a_j tensor e_i form a k-basis of A tensor_k E_0, so a tensor 1=sum_j lambda_j a_j tensor e_1=0 forces all lambda_j=0. Also A_{E_0} is finite over A, generated by 1 tensor e_1,...,1 tensor e_m. By the auxiliary claim, dim A_{E_0}=dim A=r. Since B is a subring of A_{E_0} and A_{E_0} is finite over B, the auxiliary claim also gives dim B=r. The ring B is a nonzero finitely generated E_0-algebra generated by n-1 elements, namely the images of y_1,...,y_{n-1}. By the induction hypothesis applied to B over E_0, there exist a finite field extension F/E_0 and elements z_1,...,z_r in B_F=B tensor_{E_0} F such that B_F is finite over F[z_1,...,z_r]. Tensoring the finite B-module A_{E_0} with F gives that A_F=A tensor_k F is finite over B_F. Since B_F is finite over F[z_1,...,z_r], transitivity of finiteness shows A_F is finite over F[z_1,...,z_r]. The extension F/k is finite because F is finite over E_0 and E_0 is finite over k. Finally, B_F embeds in A_F because F/E_0 is flat and B -> A_{E_0} is injective; hence the z_i are elements of A_F. Taking the desired finite extension to be F and y_i=z_i completes the induction and proves the lemma.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let Delta be the diagonal in X x X, and let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections. Let Z be a d-cycle on X x X. If for every integral component C of Z one has dim p_1(C)+dim p_2(C) <= 2d-1, then dim(Supp(Z) intersect Delta) <= d-1.
proof: Let Z = sum_i n_i C_i be a d-cycle on X x X, where the C_i are the integral d-dimensional closed subvarieties appearing with nonzero coefficient. Then Supp(Z) is the finite union of the C_i. It is enough to prove dim(C_i intersect Delta) <= d-1 for every i. Fix one such C and put D = C intersect Delta, u = dim p_1(C), v = dim p_2(C). Since p_1 and p_2 are proper morphisms X x X -> X, the images p_1(C) and p_2(C) are closed subsets of X, so u <= d and v <= d. The hypothesis gives u + v <= 2d - 1. If min(u,v) >= d, then because u,v <= d we would have u = v = d and u + v = 2d, contradicting u + v <= 2d - 1. Hence min(u,v) <= d - 1. The diagonal Delta is isomorphic to X via p_1 restricted to Delta, with inverse the diagonal morphism X -> X x X. Therefore p_1 restricted to D is a homeomorphism from D onto p_1(D), so dim D = dim p_1(D). Since p_1(D) is contained in p_1(C), dim D <= u. Similarly p_2 restricted to Delta is a homeomorphism, so dim D = dim p_2(D) <= v. Thus dim D <= min(u,v) <= d - 1. If D is empty, the inequality is also true under the usual convention dim empty = -1. Applying the argument to each component C_i, we obtain Supp(Z) intersect Delta = union_i (C_i intersect Delta), a finite union of closed subsets each of dimension at most d - 1; hence its dimension is at most d - 1. The edge case d = 0 is included: if Z had a component C, then u = v = 0, so u + v = 0, contradicting u + v <= -1; therefore Z = 0 and the conclusion holds for the empty support.

statement: Let k be a field, and let U and V be integral schemes of finite type over k. Then every irreducible component of U ×_k V has dimension dim U + dim V.
proof: We prove the statement by first proving an affine algebraic version and then gluing. We use the following standard facts. Fact A: if D is a finitely generated k-domain, then dim D = trdeg_k Frac(D). Indeed, Noether normalization gives a finite injective map k[x_1,...,x_r] -> D with r = trdeg_k Frac(D). Integral extensions preserve dimension: going-up gives dim D >= r, and incomparability gives dim D <= r. Also it is standard, from the principal ideal theorem, that dim k[x_1,...,x_r] = r; the chain (0) ⊂ (x_1) ⊂ ... ⊂ (x_1,...,x_r) gives the lower bound. Fact B: if A is a domain and B is a Noetherian flat A-algebra, then every minimal prime q of B contracts to 0 in A. Proof of Fact B: flatness over a domain implies torsion-free; if a is nonzero in A, multiplication by a is injective on A, hence injective on B. If a in q∩A were nonzero, then in the Noetherian local ring B_q the element a/1 lies in the maximal ideal. The prime ideals of B_q correspond to primes of B contained in q, and since q is minimal there are only 0 and q, so B_q has dimension 0; in a Noetherian local ring of dimension 0 the maximal ideal is nilpotent. Hence (a/1)^n = 0 for some n, so a^n s = 0 for some s not in q. Torsion-freeness over A and a^n not equal 0 force s = 0, a contradiction. We also use the standard fact that a nonempty open subset of an irreducible noetherian space has the same dimension as the whole space. Affine product lemma: let A and B be domains finitely generated over k, with a = dim A and b = dim B. Put M = A ⊗_k B. Let P be a minimal prime of M. Since B is a k-vector space, B is flat over k; for any A-module N, N⊗_A M ≅ N⊗_k B, so M is flat over A. Similarly M is flat over B. By Fact B applied to A -> M and B -> M, P∩A = 0 and P∩B = 0. Let S be the multiplicative set generated by the images of nonzero elements of A and B in M; these images are nonzero by torsion-freeness, and P∩S is empty. Localizing at S gives M_S ≅ K ⊗_k L, where K = Frac(A) and L = Frac(B), and Q is the prime of M_S corresponding to P; Q is a minimal prime of K ⊗_k L. The fraction field of M/P is the same as the fraction field of (K ⊗_k L)/Q, because localizing the domain M/P at S does not change its fraction field. We now compute the transcendence degree of Frac((K ⊗_k L)/Q). Choose transcendence bases t_1,...,t_a of K/k and u_1,...,u_b of L/k, possibly empty, and set F = k(t_1,...,t_a), G = k(u_1,...,u_b). Because K and L are finitely generated over k, K is algebraic and finitely generated over F, hence finite over F; similarly L is finite over G. The ring R = F ⊗_k G is a domain: it is a localization of k[t_1,...,t_a,u_1,...,u_b], and its fraction field is k(t_1,...,t_a,u_1,...,u_b), of transcendence degree a+b over k. Let T = F ⊗_k L. Since L is finite free over G, T is finite free over R. Since K is finite free over F, K ⊗_k L ≅ K ⊗_F T is finite free over T, hence finite free over R. Thus S_0 := K ⊗_k L is a Noetherian finite free (therefore flat) R-algebra. By Fact B, Q∩R = 0. Consequently R embeds into the domain S_0/Q, and S_0/Q is finite over R. Hence Frac(S_0/Q) is a finite algebraic extension of Frac(R), so trdeg_k Frac(S_0/Q) = trdeg_k Frac(R) = a+b. Returning to M/P, Fact A gives dim(M/P) = trdeg_k Frac(M/P) = a+b. This proves the affine product lemma. Now let U and V be integral schemes of finite type over k, and let C be an irreducible component of X = U ×_k V. Let η be the generic point of C. Choose affine open neighborhoods U_0 = Spec A and V_0 = Spec B of the images of η in U and V, respectively; then W = U_0 ×_k V_0 = Spec(A ⊗_k B) is an affine open neighborhood of η in X. Since U_0 and V_0 are nonempty affine opens of the integral schemes U and V, their coordinate rings are finitely generated k-domains with fraction fields k(U) and k(V). By Fact A, dim A = trdeg_k k(U) and dim B = trdeg_k k(V). To relate these affine dimensions to dim U and dim V, take affine open neighborhoods of the generic points of U and V; Fact A gives their dimensions equal to trdeg_k k(U) and trdeg_k k(V), and the standard open-dimension fact gives that these dimensions equal dim U and dim V. Hence dim A = dim U and dim B = dim V. The subset C∩W is closed in W and irreducible. It is dense in C because W contains η. If D is an irreducible closed subset of W containing C∩W, then the closure of D in X is an irreducible closed subset containing C; since C is an irreducible component, this closure equals C, and hence D⊂C∩W. Thus C∩W is an irreducible component of W. Therefore C∩W = Spec(M/P) for a minimal prime P of M = A ⊗_k B. By the affine product lemma, dim(C∩W) = dim(M/P) = dim A + dim B = dim U + dim V. Finally, C∩W is a nonempty open dense subset of the irreducible noetherian space C, so it has the same dimension as C. Hence dim C = dim U + dim V. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let T = k(t_1, ..., t_r) for some r >= 0, put X_T = X x_k T, and let g_T: X_T -> X and f_T: X_T x_T X_T -> X x X be the base-change morphisms. Let p_1, p_2: X x X -> X be the projections and p_{1,T}, p_{2,T}: X_T x_T X_T -> X_T the induced projections. For every alpha in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients and every i in {1,2}, one has p_{i,T*} f_T^* alpha = g_T^* p_{i*} alpha in CH^0(X_T), where f_T^* and g_T^* denote the flat pullbacks.
proof: Let T = k(t_1,...,t_r); the case r=0 is included by reading t_1,...,t_r as empty. First record two elementary facts. (1) If A is a domain that is a k-algebra, then A_T = A tensor_k T is a domain. Indeed T is the localization of k[t_1,...,t_r] at the nonzero polynomials, so A_T is the localization of A[t_1,...,t_r] at the image of those polynomials; A[t_1,...,t_r] is a domain, and a nonzero polynomial in k[t_1,...,t_r] remains nonzero in A[t_1,...,t_r] because A is a k-algebra domain. (2) If E/F is a finite field extension of degree m, then [E(t_1,...,t_r):F(t_1,...,t_r)] = m. To see this, let R=F[t_1,...,t_r]. Choosing an F-basis of E makes E[t_1,...,t_r] a free R-module of rank m. Localizing at the nonzero elements of R gives a finite free domain over F(t_1,...,t_r) of rank m, hence a field of degree m. It is identified with E(t_1,...,t_r): for 0 != v in E[t_1,...,t_r], the determinant of multiplication by v on the finite free R-module E[t_1,...,t_r] is a nonzero element of R because multiplication by v is injective (E[t_1,...,t_r] is a domain), and the inverse of v lies in the localization. Thus every element of E(t_1,...,t_r) lies in the localization, and the reverse inclusion is clear. Consequences: if Y is an integral k-scheme of finite type, then Y_T = Y x_k Spec T is integral; indeed, on an affine open Spec A with A a domain, A_T is a domain by fact (1), and the generic points of these affine opens glue because Y is irreducible. If Y has function field F, then K(Y_T)=F(t_1,...,t_r). Moreover dim Y_T = dim Y, because K(Y_T) has transcendence degree dim Y over T. In particular, let X_a run through the d-dimensional integral components of X. Since X/k is smooth, X is the disjoint union of the X_a, and each (X_a)_T is an integral d-dimensional component of X_T. We use the standard formulas for flat pullback and proper pushforward of cycles. If h: Y' -> Y is flat and V is an integral closed subscheme of Y, then h^*[V] is the associated cycle of V x_Y Y'; if V x_Y Y' is integral, this associated cycle is [V x_Y Y'] with multiplicity 1. If q is a proper morphism and V is an integral d-dimensional subvariety, then q_*[V]=0 when dim q(V)<d, and q_*[V]=[K(V):K(q(V))][q(V)] when dim q(V)=d, where q(V) is the image with reduced structure. It is enough to prove the desired equality for alpha = [W] with W an integral closed subscheme of X x X of dimension d, because every element of CH^d(X x X) is represented by a finite sum of such classes and both sides are additive in alpha. Fix i in {1,2} and such a W, and put E=K(W). Let Y=p_i(W); this is an irreducible closed subset of X because p_i is proper. Case 1: dim Y < d. By the consequence above, Y_T is integral of the same dimension as Y, hence dimension <d. The base change of the surjective morphism W -> Y is a surjective morphism W_T -> Y_T, so p_{i,T}(W_T)=Y_T has dimension <d. Since W_T is integral, f_T^*[W]=[W_T], and therefore p_{i,T*} f_T^*[W]=0. On the other hand p_{i*}[W]=0 because dim Y<d, so g_T^* p_{i*}[W]=0. Case 2: dim Y = d. Then Y is a d-dimensional irreducible closed subset of the d-dimensional smooth variety X, hence Y=X_a for one of the components X_a. Let F=K(X_a). The morphism W -> X_a is dominant, so E/F is finite; write m=[E:F]. The proper pushforward formula gives p_{i*}[W]=m[X_a]. Since (X_a)_T is integral, flat pullback gives g_T^*[X_a]=[(X_a)_T], and the right hand side is m[(X_a)_T]. For the left hand side, W_T is integral with K(W_T)=E(t_1,...,t_r), and the base change of W -> X_a shows p_{i,T}(W_T)=(X_a)_T, which has dimension d. Hence p_{i,T*} f_T^*[W] = p_{i,T*}[W_T] = [E(t_1,...,t_r):F(t_1,...,t_r)] [(X_a)_T] = m[(X_a)_T] by fact (2). Thus the two sides agree for [W]. By additivity, the equality holds for every d-cycle Z representing alpha, and therefore for alpha itself. The argument is identical for i=1 and i=2, and the case r=0 is already included. This proves p_{i,T*} f_T^* alpha = g_T^* p_{i*} alpha in CH^0(X_T).

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a finite extension of degree n, and let alpha in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients. If the flat pullback of alpha to X_L x X_L is zero and m alpha = 0 for some positive integer m with gcd(m,n)=1, then alpha = 0.
proof:
Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a finite extension of degree n, and let alpha in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients. Write res: CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_L x_L X_L) for the flat pullback induced by the base-change morphism f: X_L x_L X_L -> X x_k X, and let K = ker(res). We must show alpha = 0 under the hypotheses res(alpha) = 0 and m alpha = 0 for some positive integer m with gcd(m,n) = 1.

Step 1 (alpha lies in the kernel K). By the first hypothesis, the flat pullback of alpha to X_L x_L X_L is zero, i.e. res(alpha) = 0. Hence, by definition of K as the kernel of res, alpha in K.

Step 2 (the kernel is annihilated by n). We invoke the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_56, which states: for X/k smooth projective of dimension d, L/k a finite extension of degree n, res: CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_L x_L X_L) the flat pullback, and K = ker(res), one has n alpha = 0 in CH^d(X x_k X) for every alpha in K. For completeness we record why lemma_56 holds here: the morphism f: X_L x_L X_L -> X x_k X is the base change of the finite flat morphism Spec L -> Spec k (of degree n) along X x_k X -> Spec k, because X_L x_L X_L = (X x_k L) x_L (X x_k L) = (X x_k X) x_k L = (X x_k X)_L. Base change preserves finite flatness and degree, so f is finite flat of degree n. The projection formula for the proper (finite) morphism f, applied to beta = [(X x_k X)_L] (the fundamental class, the multiplicative unit of the Chow ring of the regular scheme (X x_k X)_L), gives f_*(f^* alpha) = f_*(f^* alpha . [(X x_k X)_L]) = alpha . f_*[(X x_k X)_L]. Since f is finite flat of degree n, f_*[(X x_k X)_L] = n [X x_k X], and hence f_*(f^* alpha) = n alpha. But f^* alpha = res(alpha) = 0 by Step 1, so 0 = f_*(f^* alpha) = n alpha. This is exactly the assertion of lemma_56, and therefore n alpha = 0 in CH^d(X x_k X).

Step 3 (combine the two annihilators via Bezout). By the second hypothesis, m alpha = 0 for a positive integer m with gcd(m, n) = 1. From Step 2 we also have n alpha = 0. Since gcd(m, n) = 1, Bezout's identity (a standard consequence of the Euclidean algorithm) provides integers a, b with a m + b n = 1. Multiplying alpha by this identity and using the module structure of the Chow group (so that (a m + b n) alpha = a (m alpha) + b (n alpha)), we obtain
  alpha = 1 . alpha = (a m + b n) . alpha = a (m alpha) + b (n alpha) = a . 0 + b . 0 = 0.
Each equality is justified: the first rewrites 1 as a m + b n; the second is distributivity of integer multiplication in the abelian group CH^d(X x_k X); the third substitutes m alpha = 0 (hypothesis) and n alpha = 0 (Step 2); the fourth is the additive identity.

Conclusion. We have shown alpha = 0 in CH^d(X x_k X), as required. This completes the proof.
